theme: Send out your light and your truth
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 43. It is a short prayer from someone in darkness, asking for God’s light and truth to lead him to worship. It pairs with Psalm 42, and it ends with a refrain of hope.
settingTheScene: Psalm 43 has no title and was likely the last stanza of Psalm 42, since they share the same refrain: “Why are you cast down, O my soul?” The singer is far from the temple, mocked by enemies and deeply discouraged. His prayer is for God to send light and truth to bring him back to worship. It follows Psalm 119 and John 8 in the theme of light and truth.
observation: “You are the God in whom I take refuge” (v. 2).
“Why do I go mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?” (v. 2).
“Send out your light and your truth; let them lead me” (v. 3).
“Let them bring me to your holy hill and to your dwelling!” (v. 3).
“Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me?” (v. 5).
“Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God” (v. 5).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a legal appeal. The singer asks God to vindicate him and defend his cause against a people who are deceitful and unjust. Then he turns to a question that many believers have asked: “For you are the God in whom I take refuge; why have you rejected me?” He is confused. God is his refuge, and yet he feels abandoned. “Why do I go mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?” The psalm lets us ask hard questions.

The center of the prayer is verse 3: “Send out your light and your truth; let them lead me.” He does not ask for an explanation of why he is suffering. He asks for light and truth, as if they were two guides sent from God. Light shows the path. Truth keeps him from deception. Together they will lead him to the holy hill and to God’s dwelling, where he can worship. John 1 and 14 tell us who God sent: Jesus is the light of the world, and he is the truth. He leads us to the Father.

The goal is worship: “Then I will go to the altar of God, to God my exceeding joy.” What he longs for is not just relief from his enemies but God himself. God is his exceeding joy. Then he will praise God with the lyre.

The psalm ends with a conversation with himself. “Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me?” He does not deny his feelings. He questions them. And he answers: “Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God.” Notice the word “again.” He is not praising now, but he knows he will. Depression and discouragement are real, and God’s people are not exempt, but they are not the last word. Our hope is in the God who will bring light.
connection: Psalm 42 shares the refrain. Psalm 27:1 and 36:9 speak of the LORD as light. Psalm 119:105 calls the word a lamp. John 1:9, 8:12, and 14:6 apply light and truth to Jesus. Lamentations 3:21-26 teaches hope in the LORD in the midst of grief. Romans 15:13 prays that the God of hope would fill you with joy and peace. 2 Corinthians 4:8-9 says we are afflicted but not crushed.
application:
When you are cast down, speak to your soul as the psalmist did. Say, “Hope in God.”

Pray verse 3 as a prayer for guidance: “Send out your light and your truth.”

Tell a trusted friend honestly if you are struggling. You do not need to carry it alone.
prayerPrompts: Tell God where you feel forgotten.
Ask him to send out his light and truth.
Tell your soul to hope in him.
